sections.h2: What do Medford, NJ homeowners typically own and earn?
sections.html:
Medford is a settled Burlington County township: owners live in 88.2 percent of its homes, and 92.8 percent of residents were in the same house a year earlier. The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 survey gives a median home value of $514,800, median household income of $157,969, median gross rent of $1,589 and 2.61 people per household. The estimated population reached 25,612 on July 1, 2025, a 4.6 percent gain over the 2020 base.

The age mix is balanced, with 21.7 percent of residents under 18 and 21.2 percent at 65 or older, and 62.2 percent of adults have a bachelor's degree or higher. Workers spend 33.9 minutes getting to their jobs on average.

sections.h2: What sets Medford's location and history apart?
sections.html:
Medford sits inside the Pinelands National Reserve, the first national reserve Congress established, in 1978, and part of the township falls in the state-designated Pinelands Area. At 38.80 square miles of land it is far more spread out than its population suggests. The independent borough of Medford Lakes sits entirely inside the township, one of New Jersey's 21 "doughnut" pairs.

Samuel Coles bought 900 acres here in 1670, and the Legislature separated Medford from Evesham Township on March 1, 1847. Glassmaking ran from the 1820s until about 1925, and nearly 30 workers' homes survive on Trimble Street and Mill Street. Local landmarks buyers recognize include:

  • Historic Medford Village, home of the Dickens Festival.
  • Kirby's Mill, a grist mill added to the national historic register.
  • Freedom Park, with playgrounds, courts, bike paths and a dog run.
  • Woodford Cedar Run Wildlife Refuge, a 170-acre preserve on the southern border.
  • The Dr. James Still Historic Office Site, preserved by the state in 2006.

Annual precipitation is about 41 inches, and snowfall averages about 23 inches. If a home sits in the Pinelands Area, ask the township zoning office what that designation means for additions, tree removal or new outbuildings before a buyer's attorney raises it.

sections.h2: How does a resale certificate of occupancy work in Medford?
sections.html:
In Medford the Fire Department handles the resale certificate of occupancy, since the construction office inspects existing housing only when someone complains. A house on public water or sewer also needs a visit from the utility billing office for a final meter reading and a sewer inspection, and wells and septic systems fall under the Burlington County Health Department, reached at 609-265-5515 in Westampton.

The fire inspection is checked against these items from the township's published requirements:

  • Working smoke detectors on every level, basements included, and within 10 feet of sleeping areas. A system installed with the house and interconnected cannot be swapped for stand-alone battery units.
  • At least one carbon monoxide detector near the bedrooms, with more where bedrooms sit on more than one level.
  • A residential fire extinguisher rated 2A-10BC, no heavier than 10 pounds, mounted no higher than 5 feet and not hidden behind a door or inside a cabinet.

The township asks sellers to leave the detector manuals for the next owner. Contact the Fire Department and the utility office early, since each needs its own visit.

sections.h2: What rules apply if the Medford house is a rental?
sections.html:
Medford runs an annual inspection program for one- and two-family rentals. Township Council Ordinance 2018-24 requires inspection every year and again at a change of use, ownership or tenancy, so a sale of a rental triggers a new inspection.

Medford rental requirements for one- and two-family houses. Source: Medford Township Construction and Inspections page.
RequirementDetail
Rental inspection$200 fee, performed by the Construction Code Office
Landlord/tenant registrationFiled with the Township Clerk, $20 application fee
Lead Safe CertificateRequired for rentals built before 1978, from a licensed testing company
Private wellWater test report every 5 years

An investor selling a rental should hand the buyer the latest inspection result, the registration and the lead certificate with the sale documents, so the new landlord can keep the property compliant from the first day.

sections.h2: What does a Medford seller owe at closing?
sections.html:
The seller owes the state realty transfer fee, which comes to about $4,317 at Medford's $514,800 median home value. The fee rises with price, and the state's own example shows a $325,000 sale at $1,910 with no exemption. Above $1,000,000, a graduated percent fee starting at 1 percent applies to the seller for deeds submitted on or after July 10, 2025.

The Burlington County Clerk records the deed. Its recordable-deed checklist calls for the names of seller and buyer, the buyer's address, the price and transfer fee, the seller's residency form (GIT/REP), the municipal block and lot, the seller's notarized signature, the preparer's printed name and a county summary sheet. The recording fee is $45 for the first page, with the summary sheet counting as that page, and $10 for each additional page. A seller claiming a fee exemption also files an Affidavit of Consideration.

sections.h2: How do roads, schools and transit shape Medford sales?
sections.html:
Route 70 is Medford's main road, joined by County Routes 532, 541 and 544, and the township maintained 153 of its 179 miles of roadway as of 2010. The old NJ Transit bus to Philadelphia that ended in Evesham has been discontinued, and Greyhound runs from nearby Mount Laurel, so most buyers plan on driving. Flying W Airport, a public-use field, sits near the Lumberton line.

Medford Township Public Schools covers pre-kindergarten through eighth grade in seven schools, with 2,517 students in 2020 to 2021. Its elementary schools are Milton H. Allen, Chairville, Cranberry Pines, Kirby's Mill and Taunton Forge, followed by the Haines Sixth Grade Center and Medford Memorial Middle School. Older students attend Shawnee High School in the Lenape Regional High School District, and Burlington County Institute of Technology has a campus in Medford. St. Mary of the Lakes School is the local Catholic option.

sections.h2: What are the choices for selling a Medford house quickly?
sections.html:
Medford owners can pick a listing agent, a private sale or a cash buyer for a house that needs work, and every route needs the Fire Department certificate and, where applicable, the utility and county health sign-offs.

  • A traditional listing suits a house in good shape and a seller who can wait for a buyer's mortgage and appraisal.
  • A private sale avoids the commission, but the owner then manages disclosures, the contract and the certificate steps without help.
  • A cash sale works for estates, rentals with tenants, houses with septic or well problems, or owners who cannot take on a month of repairs.

Compare offers on the amount left after the mortgage payoff, the transfer fee, and the cost of any repair the inspector requires.

faqs.q: Who inspects a Medford house before it sells?
faqs.a: The Medford Fire Department handles the residential resale certificate of occupancy. Homes on public water or sewer also need the utility billing office for a final meter reading and sewer inspection.

faqs.q: What if my Medford house has a well or septic system?
faqs.a: The Burlington County Health Department administers permits and inspections for wells and septic systems. Contact it at 609-265-5515 before listing so any needed work is known early.

faqs.q: Which smoke and carbon monoxide rules does Medford apply?
faqs.a: Smoke detectors are needed on every level, including basements, and within 10 feet of sleeping areas. At least one carbon monoxide detector must be near the bedrooms, and the home needs a 2A-10BC extinguisher of 10 pounds or less.

faqs.q: How much is the transfer fee on a Medford home sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays it at recording. At Medford's Census median home value of $514,800, the state schedule works out to about $4,317, and larger sales cost more.

faqs.q: Do Medford rentals need extra paperwork when sold?
faqs.a: Yes. One- and two-family rentals are inspected annually under Ordinance 2018-24 for $200, registered with the Township Clerk, and need a Lead Safe Certificate if built before 1978. Houses on wells need a water test every 5 years.
